justification_text:
The point estimates at each horizon—whether one day (1d), one week (1w), or one month (1m)—are derived from an expectation that the central tendency of the variable in question will remain constant over time, barring significant external disruptions. The figure of 273.53 likely reflects either the most current observation or an average of recent trends, adjusted for any predictable effects or seasonal patterns. This assumes that the environment driving the variable's behavior stays relatively stable across the different timeframes.

The width of the confidence intervals gets larger as the time horizon increases because uncertainty compounds over time. Over one day, there is less time for unexpected factors or cumulative randomness to cause significant deviation from the central estimate. By one week and especially by one month, more unknown variables, shifts in trends, or external shocks have had greater opportunities to affect the outcomes. Factors such as market volatility, policy changes, or the emergence of new information contribute to this rising uncertainty, which is why the confidence intervals are broader for the one-month forecast compared to the one-day forecast.

There are always risks or events that could materially alter the outcomes beyond the stated intervals. For example, sudden macroeconomic shocks, like a major interest rate announcement or geopolitical developments, could abruptly shift the underlying variable beyond the bounds of the 90% confidence interval. Structural changes in the market or system being modeled—like a sudden change in regulation or a technological breakthrough—would also create outcomes that are not captured in this probabilistic forecast. These types of events are inherently difficult to predict and are often excluded from probabilistic modeling unless explicitly accounted for.
